newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST - Coal seen fuelling JCI H1 shr.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Coal seen fuelling JCI H1 shr.

text.p: Better coal prices on world markets and a weaker currency are likely to pull up South African mining house JCI Ltd's interim profits, countering some of the dullness from gold operations, analysts said on Friday.
They said that the rand's weakness last year swelled unlisted coal unit Tavistok's export income.
"It's been quite a good year. The coal side will be much stronger because the coal prices have been up and the rand has been weaker," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
Analysts polled by Reuters forecast earnings per share in a range of 112 t0 130 cents with consensus at 124 cents per share, up from 85 cents previously.
The dividend was seen between 24 and 35 cents a share with consensus at 29.6 cents compared to 24 cents a year ago.
JCI reports results for the period ended December 31 on Wednesday.
Analysts said JCI's coal division was likely to contribute about 28 percent to the overall first half earnings.
But not everything looked jolly.
A stunted bullion price would hit profits in gold operations whose earlier glee over a much weaker rand bringing in richer rand gold prices appeared now over, analysts said.
The rand was last bid at 4.4360 on the dollar.
"Their gold earnings will be lower, pretty much flat because the rand gold price has been weaker," one analyst said.
The bullion price was last bid at $352.70 an ounce.

Nick Goodwin, mining financials analyst at Fedsure Asset Management Ltd said that he saw even worse woes ahead for JCI's gold mining stable, with the gold price looking unable to bounce over the next couple of months.
"Not a whole lot has happened in 1996. But there has really been no growth I would say," he told Reuters.
"In the second half gold is going to be worse, chrome will be about the same and coal will be down. The gold price is down quite a bit from last year. I think it's going lower," he added.

Nevertheless, JCI's gold mining stable -- Randfontein Estates, H.J. Joel Mining Co Ltd and Western Areas -- did increase profit by 17 percent to 128.24 million rand in the three months to end-September 1996.

Analysts said that the sale of Anglo American Corp's 34.9 stake in JCI to black business consortium African Mining Group (AMG) -- a deal yet to be concluded -- for 2.9 billion rand ($654m) would not affect JCI's first half results.
The consortium has until May 2, to raise the funding to close the deal which would give black business its first significant stake in the South African mining industry.
"The deal should not affect results. Operations carry on and, on the ground, nothing has changed," an analyst commented.
